newsitem.title: USA: U.S. homes less affordable in third quarter - NAR.
newsitem.headline: U.S. homes less affordable in third quarter - NAR.

text.p: Home buyers lost purchasing power during the third quarter of 1996, as rising prices and higher mortgage rates offset increases in income, the National Association of Realtors' (NAR) said Thursday.
The industry group's Housing Affordability Index dropped 1.9 percentage points to a reading of 120.0 during the third quarter from 121.9 in the second quarter.

When the NAR index stands at 100, a family earning the national median income has exactly the amount needed to buy an median priced existing home, using conventional financing and a 20 percent downpayment.
"The good news is that we're entering a buyer's market, with stabilization in both prices and interest rates," NAR President Art Godi said in a statement.

"Sales were at an all-time record in the second quarter, and now that we're easing off that peak, buyers are finding a good supply of homes, affordable prices and less competition from other buyers," Godi added.
NAR Chief Economist John Tuccillo said rates are playing a secondary role in the market. "Job growth and economic security are playing larger roles in purchase decisions," he said.
"Although home sales will ease next year, housing affordability will remain favorable," Tuccillo added.

The NAR first-time buyer index declined 1.2 percentage points to 76.3 in the third quarter. This index measures the ability of a renter aged 25 to 44 to purchase a typical starter home with a 10 percent downpayment.
Although entry-level buyers are at a relative disadvantage, the $25,275 median income of the typical first-time buyer would qualify to buy a home costing $78,100, NAR said.
The first-time buyer index showed that the income needed for conventional financing covering 90 percent of a $102,400 starter home was $33,109, which was $7,834 above the median income.
